hints.text: Ask whether any transformation at time t uses observations from after t.
Financial observations are ordered and often dependent, so random splitting can place future regimes beside past training data.

solution.setup: Inspect both preprocessing and the method used to separate training from testing.
solution.reasoning: Full-sample standardization leaks future distribution information into every past observation. A random split also trains on dates later than some test dates and ignores temporal dependence. Fit preprocessing only on each training window, evaluate on strictly later data, and use rolling or expanding walk-forward splits with a gap when labels overlap.
solution.finalAnswer: Use training-window-only preprocessing and chronological walk-forward validation; never standardize on the full sample or randomly mix future dates into training.
solution.sanityCheck: At every simulated prediction time, the corrected process uses only information that would actually have existed then.

keyInsight: A backtest is valid only if every transformation and model decision respects the historical information set.
recognitionCues: Full-sample preprocessing or random time-series splits often reveal future information.
commonMistakes: Fixing the train-test split but retaining full-sample normalization.
followUps: Why might overlapping return labels require an embargo gap?

source.notes: Original variant of a publicly reported interview family associated with Jump Trading, Two Sigma.

verification.expectedValue: training-only transforms plus chronological walk-forward evaluation
verification.notes: Both specified operations use future information; the proposed design removes them.

title: The Future-Leaking Signal
problem: A daily trading model standardizes each signal using the mean and standard deviation calculated over the entire five-year dataset, then evaluates performance with a random 80/20 train-test split. Identify the two main sources of look-ahead bias and give a valid evaluation design.
